items.title: Threats to External Validity
items.content: **Generalization targets:** External validity concerns transport across people, settings, treatments, outcomes, and times. Testing reactivity, unusual settings, restricted samples, treatment variation, and interference can limit transport, but no checklist proves or disproves generalizability. Define the target population and conditions, sample relevant heterogeneity, measure implementation, report boundaries, and use replication. Internal and external validity are not inevitably a zero-sum tradeoff.

items.title: ANOVA Types
items.content: **Choose by design and estimand:** One-way ANOVA compares modeled means across one factor; factorial ANOVA estimates main and interaction effects; repeated-measures designs model dependent observations; ANCOVA conditions on covariates under additional assumptions; MANOVA concerns multiple outcomes. Counting variables is not enough. Check independence structure, scale, residual behavior, variance assumptions, missingness, multiplicity, planned contrasts, and whether the causal interpretation is warranted.

items.title: Correlation vs Regression
items.content: **Association versus conditional model:** Correlation summarizes direction and strength of association; regression models an outcome conditional on specified predictors. In simple linear regression, squared correlation corresponds to fitted sample variance accounted for, not causal explanation. Coefficients and predictions depend on scale, functional form, collinearity, range, outliers, uncertainty, and validation. Neither method establishes causation without an appropriate design and assumptions.

items.title: Regression to the Mean
items.content: **Extreme-score retesting:** When selection uses an extreme fallible measure and repeated measurements correlate imperfectly, later scores tend on average to be less extreme. The pattern is not improvement, deterioration, or treatment response by itself. A concurrent comparison measured under the same selection process can help, but does not automatically solve selection, attrition, instrumentation, contamination, or model misspecification. Reliability, selection rule, and design determine the threat.

items.title: Reliability Types
items.content: **Precision depends on the intended score use:** Internal-consistency coefficients concern relations among item responses; test-retest evidence concerns temporal stability; interrater evidence concerns agreement or consistency among raters; alternate-form evidence concerns form comparability. A high coefficient does not prove validity, unidimensionality, fairness, or individual-score precision. Report the coefficient, design, interval, sample, conditions, uncertainty, and relevant standard error for the intended interpretation.

items.title: Factor Analysis
items.content: **Latent-structure cue:** Exploratory factor analysis estimates patterns without fixing the complete structure in advance; confirmatory factor analysis tests a prespecified measurement model. Principal components summarizes observed variance and is not identical to a common-factor model. Factor number, extraction, rotation, estimator, sample, cross-loadings, fit, and replication matter. A rotated loading pattern does not discover immutable psychological kinds or prove measurement invariance.

items.title: Chi-Square Test
items.content: **Categorical-count tests:** Goodness-of-fit compares observed counts with a specified distribution; independence or homogeneity tests compare categorical distributions across variables or groups. Expected counts, independent observations, sampling design, sparse cells, and prespecified categories matter. Statistical significance does not describe effect magnitude or causality. Report cell patterns and an appropriate association measure, and use exact or model-based alternatives when asymptotic conditions are inadequate.

items.title: Performance Rating Measurement Quality
items.content: **Treat ratings as measurement evidence:** A performance score is interpretable only for its defined job, criteria, raters, occasions, and decision use. Examine score precision, interrater consistency, criterion relevance, construct underrepresentation or contamination, subgroup fairness, range restriction, and consequences. Central clustering or disagreement may reflect scale design, opportunity to observe, real performance variation, or error; it does not by itself identify a named rater bias. Forced distributions create rather than validate a score distribution.

items.title: Scales of Measurement
items.content: **Measurement properties guide analysis:** Nominal values label categories; ordinal values add order; interval interpretations assume meaningful equal differences; ratio interpretations also posit a meaningful zero. Real measures can only approximately support these properties, and permissible analysis is not selected by the label alone. Consider the construct, coding, distribution, design, estimand, robustness, and interpretability rather than memorizing that one statistic is universally allowed or forbidden.

items.title: Correlation Pitfalls
items.content: **Inspect before interpreting r:** Pearson correlation targets linear association and can be changed by outliers, nonlinearity, range restriction, mixtures, measurement error, and dependence. A strong coefficient can coexist with poor transport or confounding; a weak coefficient can conceal subgroup or curved relations. Squaring r has a specific linear-model interpretation, not a universal percent-causal explanation. Plot data, report uncertainty, and distinguish association from direction and causation.

items.title: Normal Distribution Properties
items.content: **Normal-model cue:** A normal distribution is symmetric and determined by its mean and standard deviation; the 68-95-99.7 percentages are approximations under that model. Real data need not be normal, and mean-median-mode ordering is a heuristic rather than the definition of skewness. Kurtosis is not simply peak height. Inspect empirical distributions and residuals, use the relevant sampling model, and avoid choosing a center solely from a mnemonic.

items.title: Multivariate Statistics Overview
items.content: **Match method to question:** Multiple regression models one outcome from several predictors; logistic models categorical outcomes; MANOVA concerns multiple continuous outcomes; factor analysis addresses latent covariance structure; principal components reduces observed dimensions; discriminant methods classify under assumptions. The multivariate label does not make a method automatically superior. Sample size, dependence, scale, missing data, collinearity, multiplicity, model fit, validation, and intended inference govern selection.

items.title: Clinical vs Statistical Prediction
items.content: **Comparative prediction evidence:** Properly developed mechanical or actuarial combination often matches or exceeds unaided holistic judgment for the same criterion and information. This is probabilistic and setting-specific, not "statistics always wins." Clinicians contribute data quality, safety, feasibility, context, and information absent from a model; post-hoc overrides need evidence and documentation. Structured professional judgment is a distinct framework, and every predictive tool requires validation and monitoring in its intended population.

items.title: Type I vs Type II Errors
items.content: **Decision-error cue:** Type I error rejects a true null under a specified procedure; Type II error fails to reject a false null; power is the probability of rejection under a specified alternative. Alpha does not equal the probability that a reported finding is false, and one minus alpha is not power. Effect size, sample size, variability, design, multiplicity, assumptions, prior evidence, and consequences all shape interpretation.

items.title: ANOVA Assumptions & Post-Hocs
items.content: **ANOVA diagnostics and follow-up:** Relevant assumptions concern independence or modeled dependence, residual form, and variance structure, with robustness depending on design and sample balance. A significant omnibus test does not identify every differing pair or practical importance. Planned contrasts and multiplicity-adjusted post-hoc procedures answer different questions. Choose methods before inspecting results when possible, report effect sizes and uncertainty, and consider robust or model-based alternatives when assumptions fail.

items.title: Regression to the Mean
items.content: **Do not credit the intervention automatically:** Extreme baseline selection plus measurement error and imperfect stability produces expected movement toward the population mean on retest. The amount depends on reliability, selection threshold, and correlation across occasions. Randomized or otherwise credible concurrent comparisons help separate this artifact from change, but analysis must also address baseline imbalance, attrition, practice, history, and measurement change. Individual movement is not guaranteed.

items.title: Threats to Internal Validity
items.content: **Causal alternatives:** History, maturation, testing, instrumentation, selection, attrition, regression, contamination, and interactions can offer rival explanations for change. Random assignment and a concurrent control strengthen causal inference but do not automatically eliminate nonadherence, differential attrition, measurement problems, interference, or analysis bias. Diagnose threats from the actual assignment, timing, measurement, missingness, implementation, and estimand rather than treating "THIS MAID" as a universal checklist solution.

items.title: Nonparametric Tests
items.content: **Procedure-specific assumptions remain:** Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, Spearman, permutation, and exact tests answer different questions. They are not simply "small-sample ANOVA substitutes" or assumption-free. Independence or pairing, exchangeability, shape, ranking, ties, and sampling design matter. Some target distributions or stochastic ordering rather than medians. Compare estimands and assumptions, report effect sizes and uncertainty, and avoid claiming they are always less powerful.

items.title: Research Ethics - Belmont Report
items.content: **Three Belmont principles:** Respect for persons supports autonomy and protection for diminished autonomy; beneficence supports systematic risk-benefit assessment; justice concerns fair distribution of research burdens and benefits. Informed consent, risk review, and subject selection are applications, not the complete regulatory rule set. IRB requirements, deception, waivers, privacy, vulnerable-population protections, and withdrawal conditions depend on applicable regulation, protocol, and setting.
